title: DTFT, DFT & FFT
description: Describe sequences in frequency with the DTFT, compute DFTs by hand and see why the FFT is fast.

study.title: The DTFT
study.body: The discrete-time Fourier transform gives the spectrum of a sequence as a continuous function of the digital frequency $\Omega$ in rad/sample. Since $e^{-j(\Omega+2\pi)n} = e^{-j\Omega n}$, $X(\Omega)$ is **periodic**, with period $2\pi$: only $-\pi < \Omega \le \pi$ is unique, and $\Omega = \pi$ means $f_s/2$. It is the z-transform on the unit circle, $z = e^{j\Omega}$; for samples $x(nT)$, $\Omega = \omega T$. Explore $a^n u[n]$: low-pass for $a > 0$, high-pass for $a < 0$.

study.title: DTFT pairs
study.body: $\delta[n] \leftrightarrow 1$: all frequencies equally. $a^n u[n] \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{1-ae^{-j\Omega}}$ for $|a| < 1$. A rectangular pulse of $N$ ones, from $n = 0$ to $N-1$, gives the **digital sinc** (Dirichlet kernel): peak $N$ at $\Omega = 0$, first nulls at $\pm 2\pi/N$, and unlike the CT sinc it repeats every $2\pi$. Longer pulse, narrower spectrum.

study.title: DTFT properties
study.body:
- Linearity: $ax_1 + bx_2 \leftrightarrow aX_1 + bX_2$
- Time shift: $x[n-n_0] \leftrightarrow e^{-j\Omega n_0}X(\Omega)$; the magnitude is unchanged
- Frequency shift: $e^{j\Omega_0 n}x[n] \leftrightarrow X(\Omega - \Omega_0)$
- Real $x[n]$: $X(-\Omega) = X^*(\Omega)$, so $|X|$ is even and $\angle X$ odd
- Convolution: $x[n]*h[n] \leftrightarrow X(\Omega)H(\Omega)$
- Parseval: energy is the same in both domains

study.title: The DFT
study.body: Take a record of $N$ samples and sample its DTFT at $N$ frequencies $\Omega_k = 2\pi k/N$: that is the DFT. Bin $k$ is at $f_k = kf_s/N$, and $X[0]$ is the plain sum of the samples. For real $x[n]$, $X[N-k] = X^*[k]$, so only bins $0 \ldots N/2$ carry new information. Explore: $L$ ones in an 8-point record; the dots are the DFT, the grey curve the DTFT.

study.title: Inverse DFT and periodicity
study.body: The inverse DFT has the same form with $+j$ and a factor $1/N$. Both $x[n]$ and $X[k]$ from these sums repeat with period $N$: the DFT treats the record as **one period of a periodic sequence**. This is the discrete-time Fourier series: a sequence with period $N$ has a line spectrum at $\Omega_k = 2\pi k/N$ with coefficients $X[k]/N$. Shorthand: $W_N = e^{-j2\pi/N}$, so $X[k] = \sum x[n]W_N^{kn}$.

study.title: The FFT
study.body: A direct DFT costs $N^2$ complex multiplications. Radix-2 decimation in time splits the record into even- and odd-indexed samples, takes a DFT of length $N/2$ of each, $E[k]$ and $O[k]$, and combines them with **butterflies**. Repeated, that gives $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies, one twiddle multiplication $W_N^k$ each. For $N = 1024$: 1 048 576 versus 5120 multiplications, a speed-up of 205.

steps.title: The DTFT
steps.body: The **discrete-time Fourier transform** describes the frequency content of a sequence. Each sample is weighted by $e^{-j\Omega n}$, where $\Omega$ is the digital frequency in **rad/sample**. Setting $z = e^{j\Omega}$ in the z-transform gives the same sum: the DTFT is $X(z)$ on the unit circle.

steps.prompt: The DTFT $X(\Omega)$ of every sequence repeats itself every $2\pi$ rad/sample.
steps.explanation: $e^{-j(\Omega + 2\pi)n} = e^{-j\Omega n}e^{-j2\pi n} = e^{-j\Omega n}$ because $n$ is an integer. So every term, and therefore $X(\Omega)$, is periodic with period $2\pi$. This is aliasing seen from the frequency side: $\Omega$ and $\Omega + 2\pi$ are the same sequence frequency.

steps.prompt: The sequence $x[n] = ({{a}})^n u[n]$ has DTFT $X(\Omega) = \frac{1}{1 - ae^{-j\Omega}}$.

ask.explanation: At $\Omega = 0$, $e^{-j0} = 1$: $X(0) = \frac{1}{1-a}$ = 1/(1 − ({{a}})) = {{1/(1-a)}}. (This is also $\sum x[n]$, the sum of all samples.)
At $\Omega = \pi$, $e^{-j\pi} = -1$: $X(\pi) = \frac{1}{1+a}$ = 1/(1 + ({{a}})) = {{1/(1+a)}}. With $a > 0$ this is smaller than $X(0)$ (low-pass); with $a < 0$ larger (high-pass).

steps.title: Link with the analog spectrum
steps.body: If $x[n] = x(nT)$ comes from sampling, the DTFT is the spectrum of the sampled signal: the analog spectrum scaled by $1/T$ and repeated every $f_s$. Digital and analog frequency are linked by $\Omega = \omega T$, so $\Omega = 2\pi$ is $f_s$ and $\Omega = \pi$ is the Nyquist frequency $f_s/2$.

steps.prompt: A sampled signal ($f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}) has a DTFT with a sharp peak at $\Omega$ = {{W}} rad/sample. Which analog frequency does the peak represent?
$x[n] = a^n u[n]$. Set $a$ so that $|X(0)|$ is {{R}} times $|X(\pi)|$.
steps.explanation: $|X(0)|/|X(\pi)| = \frac{1/(1-a)}{1/(1+a)} = \frac{1+a}{1-a}$. Setting this to {{R}} gives $a = \frac{R-1}{R+1}$ = {{(R-1)/(R+1)}}. A positive $a$ makes a low-pass spectrum, a negative $a$ a high-pass one.

steps.title: The DFT
steps.body: A computer cannot store the continuous $X(\Omega)$. Instead take $N$ samples and evaluate their DTFT at $N$ frequencies $\Omega_k = 2\pi k/N$: the **discrete Fourier transform**. With sampling rate $f_s$, bin $k$ lies at $f_k = kf_s/N$, and bins above $N/2$ are the negative frequencies.

steps.prompt: A real signal sampled at {{fs|Hz}} is analysed with an $N$ = {{N||5}}-point DFT.

ask.prompt: At which frequency does bin $k$ = {{k}} lie?
A tone gives a peak in bin {{k}}. In which other bin does its mirror image appear?
ask.explanation: For real signals $X[N-k] = X^*[k]$, so the same magnitude appears in bin $N - k$ = {{N||5}} − {{k}} = {{N-k}}. That bin represents the negative frequency $-f_k$.

steps.prompt: A 4-point DFT is taken of $x[n] = [{{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}, {{d}}]$. What is $X[0]$?
steps.explanation: For $k = 0$ every exponential is $e^0 = 1$, so $X[0] = \sum x[n]$ = {{a}} + {{b}} + {{c}} + {{d}} = {{S}}. It is $N$ times the mean ({{S/4}}). $a - b + c - d$ would be $X[2]$.

steps.prompt: Match each sequence to its DTFT.
steps.explanation: A unit sample has a flat spectrum (1); delaying it by 3 adds the linear phase $e^{-j3\Omega}$. $a^n u[n]$ gives $1/(1-ae^{-j\Omega})$. Multiplying by $e^{j\Omega_0 n}$ shifts the spectrum by $\Omega_0$ (frequency shift, modulation).

steps.prompt: Compute the 2-point DFT of $x[n] = [{{a}}, {{b}}]$.

ask.explanation: For $N = 2$: $e^{-j\pi} = -1$, so $X[1] = x[0] - x[1]$ = {{a}} − ({{b}}) = {{a-b}}. This sum/difference pair is the basic FFT butterfly.

steps.prompt: Compute the 4-point DFT of $x[n] = [{{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}, {{d}}]$. Use $W_4 = e^{-j\pi/2} = -j$.
A real sequence of $N = 8$ samples has $X[{{k}}] = {{p}} + j{{q}}$. What is $X[{{8-k}}]$?
steps.explanation: For real $x[n]$: $X[N-k] = X^*[k]$. Bin {{8-k}} = 8 − {{k}} is the mirror of bin {{k}}, so it is the complex conjugate: {{p}} − j{{q}}. Same magnitude, opposite phase.

steps.prompt: An inverse 4-point DFT: $X[k] = [{{A}}, {{B}}, {{C}}, {{B}}]$ (all real).
$x[n] = [{{a}}, {{b}}, {{a}}]$ for $n = 0, 1, 2$ (zero elsewhere). Its DTFT is $X(\Omega) = e^{-j\Omega}(b + 2a\cos\Omega)$.

ask.explanation: $|e^{-j\Omega}| = 1$, so $|X| = |b + 2a\cos\Omega|$. At $\Omega = 0$: {{b}} + 2·{{a}} = {{b+2*a}} (the sum of the samples).

steps.prompt: $y[n] = x[n - {{n0}}]$. How is $|Y(\Omega)|$ related to $|X(\Omega)|$?
steps.explanation: Time shift: $Y(\Omega) = e^{-j{{n0}}\Omega}X(\Omega)$. The factor has magnitude 1, so only the phase changes (by $-{{n0}}\Omega$, linear in frequency). A shift in **frequency** would come from multiplying by $e^{j\Omega_0 n}$.

steps.prompt: $x[n] = [{{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}, {{d}}]$. Without computing the DFT, find $\sum_{k=0}^{3}|X[k]|^2$.
For a **real** sequence with $N = 8$, $X[4]$ is always real.
steps.explanation: $X[4] = \sum x[n]e^{-j\pi n} = \sum x[n](-1)^n$, a sum of real numbers. Equivalently $X[N-k] = X^*[k]$ with $k = N/2$ gives $X[4] = X^*[4]$. The same holds for $X[0]$.

steps.title: Decimation in time
steps.body: Split $x[n]$ into even samples $x[0], x[2], \ldots$ and odd samples $x[1], x[3], \ldots$ and take an $N/2$-point DFT of each: $E[k]$ and $O[k]$. One **butterfly** then gives two outputs with a single twiddle multiplication $W_N^k = e^{-j2\pi k/N}$. Repeating the split until 2-point DFTs remain gives $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies.

steps.prompt: Compare a direct DFT and a radix-2 FFT for $N$ = {{N||5}}.

ask.prompt: How many complex multiplications does the direct DFT need?
How many complex multiplications does the FFT need?
What is the speed-up factor (DFT count / FFT count)?

steps.prompt: Put the steps of an 8-point decimation-in-time FFT in order.
items: Reorder the input in bit-reversed order: x[0], x[4], x[2], x[6], …
Stage 2: combine into two 4-point DFTs using $W_4$ twiddles
Stage 3: combine into the 8-point DFT using $W_8^0 \ldots W_8^3$
steps.explanation: Repeated even/odd splitting scrambles the input order (bit reversal: index 1 = 001 becomes 100 = 4). Then $\log_2 8 = 3$ stages of 4 butterflies each build 2-point, 4-point and finally the 8-point DFT.

steps.prompt: A record of {{M||4}} samples is zero-padded to the next power of 2 for a radix-2 FFT.

ask.prompt: How many complex multiplications does the FFT need?
ask.explanation: $N$ = {{N||5}} = $2^{{{m}}}$, so $\frac{N}{2}\log_2 N$ = {{N/2||5}} × {{m}} = {{N/2*m||6}}. A direct {{M||4}}-point DFT would need {{M^2/1e6}} million.

steps.prompt: A processor needs {{tc|s}} per complex multiplication. Estimate the time for an $N$ = {{N||5}}-point transform (count multiplications only).

ask.explanation: $N^2 = 2^{ {{2*m}} } \approx {{mant||3}} \times 10^{ {{ex}} }$ multiplications × {{tc|s}} = {{N^2*tc|s}}, {{2*N/m}} times longer than the FFT.

steps.prompt: Find the twiddle factor $W_8^{{{k}}} = e^{-j2\pi \cdot {{k}}/8}$.
The FFT is a fast **approximation** of the DFT: it trades a small error for speed.
steps.explanation: The FFT computes **exactly** the same $X[k]$ as the DFT sum (apart from rounding). It only reorganises the computation so that shared partial sums are reused; that is where the saving from $N^2$ to $\frac{N}{2}\log_2 N$ comes from.

steps.prompt: Which property of the twiddle factors makes the butterfly work, i.e. lets $X[k]$ and $X[k+N/2]$ share one multiplication?
steps.explanation: $W_N^{N/2} = e^{-j\pi} = -1$, so $W_N^{k+N/2} = -W_N^k$. The product $W_N^k O[k]$ is computed once, then added for $X[k]$ and subtracted for $X[k+N/2]$. (The other statements are true but are not what saves the multiplication.)

steps.prompt: $x[n] = {{A}}\cos(2\pi \cdot {{m}}n/{{N||5}})$ for $n = 0 \ldots {{N-1}}$ is transformed with an $N$ = {{N||5}}-point DFT.

ask.explanation: $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}(e^{j\theta} + e^{-j\theta})$. The record holds exactly {{m}} cycles, so each half lands in a single bin with weight $N \cdot A/2$: $|X[{{m}}]|$ = {{N||5}} × {{A}}/2 = {{A*N/2}}.

ask.prompt: Which other bin $k$ (between 0 and $N-1$) is nonzero?
ask.explanation: The $e^{-j\theta}$ half sits at $-{{m}}$, which the periodic DFT shows at $N - m$ = {{N||5}} − {{m}} = {{N-m}}, with the same magnitude {{A*N/2}}.

steps.prompt: A spectrum analyser takes an $N$ = {{N||5}}-point DFT at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}} (rectangular window). The only peak is $|X[{{k}}]|$ = {{P||5}} (and its mirror). The tone lies exactly on the bin.

ask.prompt: Find the amplitude of the tone.
ask.explanation: A cosine of amplitude $A$ gives $|X[k]| = AN/2$, so $A = 2|X[k]|/N$ = 2 × {{P||5}} / {{N||5}} = {{2*P/N}}.

steps.prompt: $x[n] = {{D}} + {{A}}\cos(2\pi n/4)$ for $n = 0 \ldots 7$ is transformed with an 8-point DFT.

ask.explanation: $X[0] = \sum x[n]$. The cosine completes two whole cycles and sums to zero, so $X[0] = 8D$ = 8 × {{D}} = {{8*D}}.
$\cos(2\pi n/4) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 2n/8)$: two cycles in 8 samples, bin 2. $|X[2]| = NA/2$ = 8 × {{A}}/2 = {{4*A}} (the other half is in bin 6).

steps.prompt: A pulse of $L$ = {{L}} ones is zero-padded to $N$ = {{N||5}} samples. The DFT samples the digital sinc: $|X[k]| = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi Lk/N)}{\sin(\pi k/N)}\right|$. Find $|X[{{k}}]|$.
steps.explanation: $|X[{{k}}]| = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi \cdot {{L}} \cdot {{k}}/{{N||5}})}{\sin(\pi \cdot {{k}}/{{N||5}})}\right|$ = |{{sin(pi*L*k/N)}} / {{sin(pi*k/N)}}| = {{abs(sin(pi*L*k/N)/sin(pi*k/N))}}. Compare $X[0] = L$ = {{L}}: the DFT just picks points off the DTFT of the pulse.

steps.prompt: A real-time analyser at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}} computes an $N$ = {{N||5}}-point FFT of every new block of $N$ samples. A complex multiplication takes {{tc|s}}. Which percentage of the time does the processor spend on FFT multiplications?
steps.explanation:
FFT time: $\frac{N}{2}\log_2 N \cdot t$ = {{N/2*m||6}} × {{tc|s}} = {{N/2*m*tc|s}}.
A new block arrives every $N/f_s$ = {{N/fs|s}}.
Load = {{N/2*m*tc|s}} / {{N/fs|s}} = {{100*N/2*m*tc/(N/fs)|%}}. (A direct DFT would need {{2*N/m}} times more.)

steps.prompt: The $N$ = {{N||5}}-point DFT of $x[n]$ has a peak in bin $k$ = {{k}}. In which bin (0 to $N-1$) does this peak appear in the DFT of $(-1)^n x[n]$?
steps.explanation: $(-1)^n = e^{j\pi n}$: a frequency shift by $\Omega_0 = \pi$, which is $N/2$ bins. Bin $k$ moves to $k + N/2$ = {{k}} + {{N/2}}, taken modulo {{N||5}}: {{mod(k+N/2,N)}}. This trick turns a low-pass spectrum into a high-pass one.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows $|X(\Omega)|$ of $x[n] = (-0.7)^n u[n]$?
steps.explanation: $|X(\Omega)| = 1/|1 + 0.7e^{-j\Omega}|$: at $\Omega = 0$ it is 1/1.7 = 0.59, at $\Omega = \pm\pi$ it is 1/0.3 = 3.3. A negative $a$ alternates the sign of the samples, so the energy sits at high frequencies, and the plot repeats every $2\pi$.
